narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 57.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile after your first year and the bottom decile after your third year, far below the average performance of students who were accepted. These low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that is strongly associated with not passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 worked in the opposite direction. It is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing, but not enough to overcome the effect of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 33 also nudged the outcome slightly toward passing compared with the model’s expectations, yet its influence was smaller than the other two factors.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic performance trajectory made success on the bar exam less likely than the average applicant.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking courses, seeking academic support, or gaining additional legal experience could help demonstrate a clearer upward trend before you reapply.
